drills.label: Cold open
drills.question_line: SAM: Here is your opening item. A consultant asks Claude to "write a project update"
drills.stem: A consultant asks Claude to "write a project update" for a client's steering committee. The draft is long, generic and leads with activity rather than decisions. What is the most effective next prompt?

options.A: Repeat the request and add "make it excellent, concise and professional"
options.B: Name the readers and their 10 minutes, the phase two budget decision, the 3 things to cover, 1 page, and attach this month's notes
options.C: Switch to the most capable model and repeat the request
options.D: Attach every project document from the last six months

drills.why: Generic output means missing audience and purpose. A adds adjectives, not information; C pays to guess at the same gaps; D is volume in place of specificity.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. Choose two. A finance analyst asks Claude to explain
drills.stem: Choose two. A finance analyst's variance explanation for regional managers runs to 3 pages of accounting terms, and the managers don't read past page one. Which two prompt changes most directly fix it?

options.A: State the readers have no finance training and will use it to decide where to cut spend
options.B: Ask for 1 page, the 3 biggest drivers first, each with a plain line on what the manager can do
options.D: Ask Claude to rate its confidence at the end

drills.why: A fixes the level, B the length and shape. C names no gap; D trusts self-reported confidence; E: the data is in the file, not on the web.

drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. For each request, choose one prompt or a chain of stages.
drills.answer_line: ALEX: One prompt, chain, one prompt, chain.
drills.prompt: One prompt or a chain? 1. Rewrite a 2-paragraph supplier email in a warmer tone. 2. 40 interview transcripts to themes, then a recommendations memo; the director approves themes first. 3. Translate a short internal notice into Spanish. 4. Tender response: extract requirements, match capabilities, flag gaps, draft.
drills.answer: 1 one prompt. 2 chain. 3 one prompt. 4 chain.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A sales lead uses the same prompt every Monday
drills.stem: A sales lead's weekly account summaries keep leaving out contract renewal dates. Adding "please be thorough" changed nothing. What is the best next step?

options.A: Regenerate each summary until one includes the renewal date
options.B: Make renewal date a required output field, add one finished example, test on last week's accounts
options.C: Move to the most capable model, since it will be more thorough
options.D: Stop using Claude and write the summaries by hand

drills.why: The instruction never asked for the field. A repeats the gamble weekly, C is the bigger-model distractor, D abandons a task a small change fixes.

drills.label: Drill
drills.question_line: SAM: Pause here and answer before we go on. A communications lead wants ideas for an internal campaign
drills.stem: A communications lead wants ideas for an internal campaign to raise uptake of a new expenses tool. Which approach fits the task best?

options.A: Ask for the single best campaign with a full rollout plan
options.B: Ask for 20 distinct ideas across channels and tones, then shortlist 3 against budget and audience
options.C: Run research mode on other companies' campaigns and adopt the top result
options.D: Write a detailed template for tone, length and channel, and ask for one idea that fits

drills.why: Brainstorming: go wide, then converge against criteria. A and D collapse to one idea; C copies instead of generating for this audience.

drills.question_line: SAM: Your turn. Pause and name the four objectives we covered
drills.answer_line: ALEX: Effective prompts, with audience, purpose and format.
drills.prompt: Name the four objectives we covered, and the habit that goes with each.
drills.answer: Effective prompts: audience, purpose, format. Decomposition: chain when stages need checking. Iteration: one change at a time. Task type: a different approach for analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming.

In this episode: Give Claude the audience, purpose and shape of the answer
Decide when a big request becomes a chain
Improve a prompt one change at a time
Switch approach for analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming
Cold open: the steering committee update: Treat Claude as a brilliant new employee who lacks your context
Golden rule: would a colleague with minimal context follow it?
Give the reason behind a constraint; Claude generalises from it
Say what to do, not what not to do
Examples steer format and tone; start with one
Breaking a task into stages: One prompt asking too much drops parts or does them thinly
A chain: each prompt does one stage, output feeds the next
Check each stage before building on it
Numbered steps when order or completeness matters
Self-correction: draft, review against criteria, revise
Iterating a prompt: The first prompt rarely works perfectly
Decide what good looks like before you start
Name the specific gap; change one thing at a time
Ask for the change, not for suggestions
Matching the approach to the task: Analysis: long material first, question after; quotes before conclusions
Research: success criteria, check claims across sources
Web search: 1-2 lookups. Research mode: 5+ lookups, 1-3 minutes, cited report
Extended thinking: complex reasoning without recent web information
Drafting: audience, purpose, tone, length, house-style example, supplied facts
Brainstorming wants range; heavy constraints up front narrow it
Cold open: the verdict: Answer: B, reader, decision, contents, length and the right notes
Six months of documents buries this month's status
Some of it may be data policy says not to share
Adjectives add no information; a bigger model guesses the same gaps
Five to remember: Write for a brilliant newcomer: task, audience, purpose, reasons, shape, labelled material
Say what to do; one example first; permit "data is insufficient"
Chain distinct stages or checkpoints; escalate cross-system automation
Name the gap, change one thing, test on real cases
Match the approach: analysis, research, drafting, brainstorming
Recap: the exam tells: Generic or wrong reader → audience, purpose and format
Every document, all the history → volume dressed up as context
Parts dropped or a stage to approve → chain
Must run automatically across systems → escalate
Same gap every week → change the prompt and test it
One current fact → web search; cited comparison → research mode
Ideas or options → wide first, narrow second
